newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ committee wants changes to EQC forex risk mgt.
newsitem.headline: NZ committee wants changes to EQC forex risk mgt.

text.p: Parliament's finance and expenditure committee wants the government to let the Earthquake Commission (EQC) manage its own foreign exchange risk, perhaps through a paper transaction that would not increase the government's overall exposure.
Committee chairman Tony Ryall said on Tuesday that if EQC was able to operate this way the changes would align responsibility and accountability.

"The EQC would enter into foreign exchange management contracts on paper with the Debt Management Office (of Treasury). Therefore, we would be aligning control and accountability but the government's overall position would be unchanged," Ryall told Reuters in a telephone interview.
"There is also concern the EQC has to carry the foreign exchange losses even though they don't manage the situation.
"We have said this is ultimately a decision of the government ... but it should consider being more flexible in its approach," Ryall said.

Under a directive from Finance Minister Bill Birch the EQC, which collects premiums from homeowners and partially insures them against some natural disasters, is not allowed to hedge its foreign currency exposure.
Government sources said legislation was being prepared which would clarify the impact of ministers' directives.
The government believes netting the Crown's overall foreign assets against liabilities provides a natural hedge against foreign exchange risk.
In 1993 the EQC converted some funds to Reserve Bank Foreign Bond Linked Notes (FBLNs) but the rising New Zealand dollar has meant the EQC has suffered revaluation losses of $170 million.
The FBLNs had a value of $787 million at June 1996.
Ryall said a more straightforward option than the paper deal with the Debt Management Office would be for the EQC to unwind the FBLNs altogether.
He said the committee had also made the point the government should rethink putting so much of EQC's assets into government securities.
"The very people that will have to be called on to meet those securities are also going to be stretched in the case of a major earthquake anyway," Ryall said.
EQC officials had told the committee a prudent approach would be to invest almost all the natural disaster fund offshore.
